title: Navratri to Dussehra: The Inner Enemy
intro: Ten verses from the Bhagavad Gita on the enemy within, through the nine nights of Navratri to Dussehra.

posts.caption: For many, Navratri, nine nights honouring the goddess Durga, begins today, leading to Dussehra and the victory of good over evil. Until then, verses from the Gita on the enemy within. Arjuna has asked what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna's answer is desire and anger, born of rajas, the restless quality of nature.

Krishna compares desire to a fire that is never satisfied, however much fuel it is fed, and says it clouds the wisdom of even the wise as their constant enemy. The point is that indulging desire does not end it; it only feeds it. During Navratri, many fast or eat simply, a traditional way of steadying the senses for nine days.

Krishna has named the senses, mind and intellect as desire's strongholds, and his strategy starts with the senses, the outer gates. Bharatarshabha, "bull among the Bharatas," is one of Arjuna's many epithets. In Navratri stories the goddess fights her battles outwardly; the battle Krishna describes is fought within.

A ladder of inner faculties: above the senses is the mind (manas), above the mind the intellect (buddhi), and above all, the self. The Katha Upanishad, which the Gita often echoes, describes a similar ladder. Knowing what is highest, Krishna says next, gives strength against desire.

Chapter 3 ends with a call to conquer an inner enemy by steadying the self through the higher Self. Some read Navratri's battles the same way, with the goddess's victory over demons standing for the mind's victory over its own darker forces.

Desire chases satisfaction outward, and in chapter 5 Krishna points the other way: one unattached to "external contacts," the meeting of the senses with their objects, finds joy within. The next verse calls pleasures born of such contacts "wombs of pain," because they begin and end.

Near its end, chapter 5 pictures the sage in meditation, senses, mind and intellect held steady: the same three Krishna named in chapter 3 as desire's strongholds. Free of desire, fear and krodha, anger (Besant's "passion"), such a person is liberated; the Sanskrit ends sada mukta eva sah, "ever free indeed."

posts.display: Let him raise the self by the Self and not let the self become depressed; for verily is the Self the friend of the self, and also the Self the self's enemy.
posts.caption: For many, Durga Ashtami, the eighth day of Navratri, falls around now. In chapter 6, Krishna says each person must lift themselves up by their own effort and not drag themselves down, for one's own self can be one's best friend or worst enemy. The point is that the inner battle is fought, and won, from within. The Sanskrit plays on atman, meaning both "oneself" and "the Self"; Besant's capitals mark the higher sense.

With the self mastered, Krishna says, one stays steady through cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour: the calm of someone who has won the inner battle. For many, Maha Navami falls today, and in much of South India Ayudha Puja falls today or tomorrow, honouring the tools, books and instruments of one's work.

Happy Dussehra. Vijayadashami, "the tenth day of victory," celebrates Rama's victory over Ravana and, for many, Durga's over the buffalo demon Mahishasura; in much of North India, effigies of Ravana burn at dusk. The Gita names the enemies within: lust, anger and greed, three gates to ruin, to be given up. Thank you for keeping these nights with us.
